dataflow.summary: HTTP form or Basic credentials -> token route -> bcrypt verification

impact.why: A guessed professional credential exposes health scheduling data; high-volume bcrypt work can also disrupt appointment operations.

likelihood.why: Credential stuffing and request flooding require only network reachability.

reachability.summary: Both endpoints are public by design and require no prior token.

attackPath.summary: An unauthenticated network client repeatedly posts passwords, MFA codes, or client secrets until credentials succeed or bcrypt work consumes available workers.

codeEvidence.explanation: Attacker-controlled credentials reach bcrypt verification on every request; no rate dependency, cooldown, or lockout is present.
codeEvidence.label: Password endpoint directly verifies every request

codeEvidence.explanation: The laboratory secret can also be guessed without a request budget, and every attempt performs an expensive bcrypt check.
codeEvidence.label: Client Credentials endpoint shares the same missing limit

confidence.rationale: Both externally reachable token handlers invoke bcrypt-backed authentication without any application-level request limiter or lockout.

preventiveControls: Define every public route's resource budget centrally and alert on repeated authentication failures.
findings.remediation: Apply centralized per-client rate limits with stricter budgets for human and M2M token endpoints, return 429 with Retry-After, and use a distributed limiter at production scale.
remediationTests: Send attempts up to the login budget and assert the next request receives 429.
Verify ordinary API routes use a higher request budget.

rootCause.summary: The token routes enforce credential correctness but no consumption policy. Because bcrypt intentionally costs CPU, an attacker can combine credential guessing with application-level resource exhaustion.

findings.summary: Remote clients can submit unlimited password, MFA, and client-secret guesses to both token endpoints, enabling credential stuffing and CPU exhaustion against the healthcare API.

taxonomy.category: OWASP API4:2023 Unrestricted Resource Consumption / API2:2023 Broken Authentication

findings.title: Unlimited token attempts permit credential attacks and bcrypt resource exhaustion

assertions: Every syntactically valid attempt reaches authentication.
The same missing control affects the unlisted M2M sibling endpoint.
limitations: No load test was run against the development machine.
validation.summary: The route dependencies and application middleware were reviewed; neither endpoint has a limiter and `app/main.py` installs no rate-limiting middleware.

dataflow.summary: previously issued JWT -> signature validation -> claims-only Principal -> protected route

impact.why: The residual token can read protected scheduling data within its existing role and ownership.

likelihood.why: The path depends on prior token issuance or theft and a later deactivation event.

reachability.attacker: disabled account holder or token thief
reachability.outcome: continued access during the residual session window
reachability.summary: Requires a still-unexpired token; no administrator privilege is required after the token has been obtained.

attackPath.summary: A user or service obtains a token, is disabled after suspected compromise, and continues calling protected routes until `exp`.

codeEvidence.explanation: A valid signature is treated as sufficient current authority; the user/client record is never loaded after token issuance.
codeEvidence.label: Principal is reconstructed only from JWT claims

codeEvidence.code:
is_active: bool = Field(default=True)
...
class OAuthClient(SQLModel, table=True):
    ...
    is_active: bool = Field(default=True)
codeEvidence.explanation: The data model provides a revocation decision, but protected requests do not consult it.
codeEvidence.label: Persistent identities already expose active-state flags

confidence.rationale: The principal builder has no database dependency while both persistent identity models expose an `is_active` revocation flag.

preventiveControls: Add a token-version or revocation mechanism if immediate per-token invalidation is required beyond account status.
findings.remediation: Resolve the token subject against the database on protected requests, reject inactive or missing users and clients, and verify role, professional link, and allowed scopes still match current state.
remediationTests: Issue a token, deactivate its user, and assert the next protected request returns 401.
Repeat for a disabled OAuth client.

rootCause.summary: The authorization boundary uses a self-contained JWT but omits a current-state lookup. Disabling an identity affects future token issuance only, not already-issued bearer tokens.

findings.summary: Bearer-token validation trusts identity, role, ownership attributes, and scopes from the signed JWT without checking whether the backing user or OAuth client remains active.
findings.title: Disabled users and OAuth clients retain access until JWT expiry

assertions: A previously issued token remains cryptographically valid for the configured 30-minute lifetime after deactivation.
limitations: Exploitation requires possession of a token issued before deactivation.
validation.summary: Token issuance checks `is_active`, while protected-request principal construction does not query either identity table.

dataflow.summary: HTTP request -> FastAPI route -> response without hardening headers

impact.why: Framing or downgrade-related conditions can support attacks on an authenticated clinical workflow.

likelihood.why: Exploitability depends on browser session behavior and deployment topology not present in the repository.

reachability.entrypoint: reception HTML or any API response
reachability.summary: Requires the application to be deployed without a compensating edge policy.

attackPath.summary: A browser visits the reception view through a deployment lacking compensating proxy headers; an attacker can frame the page or benefit from weaker transport/content-type policy.

codeEvidence.code:
app = FastAPI(...)
app.include_router(health.router)
app.include_router(auth.router, prefix="/api/v1")
app.include_router(appointments.router, prefix="/api/v1")
app.include_router(reception.router)
codeEvidence.explanation: No middleware or response hook adds Strict-Transport-Security, X-Frame-Options, or X-Content-Type-Options.
codeEvidence.label: Application registers routers without response hardening

confidence.rationale: Application construction installs no response-security middleware and the repository contains no proxy or deployment manifest that supplies the headers.

preventiveControls: Keep a single header policy in application middleware and verify equivalent edge configuration during deployment.
findings.remediation: Add centralized middleware that sets HSTS, X-Frame-Options: DENY, and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff on every response, with production TLS enforced at the edge.
remediationTests: Assert all representative JSON and HTML responses include the three required headers.

rootCause.summary: HTTP hardening is neither application-owned nor defined in a deployment manifest, so every response lacks the required defense-in-depth headers in the current runnable configuration.

findings.summary: The FastAPI application returns API and reception HTML responses without HSTS, frame restrictions, or MIME-sniffing protection, leaving deployment safety dependent on undocumented external infrastructure.
findings.title: Responses omit required transport and browser hardening headers

assertions: Clients receive no application-declared HSTS or nosniff policy.
limitations: An external production proxy could add these headers, but no such configuration was supplied.
validation.summary: All application setup and root configuration files were reviewed; no alternate header-enforcement layer exists in the repository.
